name: Dolly Parton
description:
'''Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean''' ({{nee|'''Parton'''}}; January 19, 1946 – August 25, 2026) was an American singer-songwriter, actress and businesswoman. Dubbed the "[[Queen of country|Queen of Country]]", Parton was one of the most successful [[country music]] performers in history. She was also known for her [[Cultural impact of Dolly Parton|cultural influence]] and [[Philanthropy and advocacy of Dolly Parton|philanthropy]], particularly through [[Dollywood]] and the [[Dollywood Foundation]]. With more than 100 million records sold, Parton is among the [[list of best-selling music artists|best-selling music artists]] ever.

Born into poverty in rural [[Tennessee]], Parton wrote her first song at age six, performed regularly on television by age ten, made her first recording a year later, and became a professional songwriter at sixteen. After writing songs for others, she released her debut album, ''[[Hello, I'm Dolly]]'' in 1967, starting her nearly 60-year career. Parton released [[Dolly Parton albums discography|49 studio albums]] and wrote more than 3,000 songs, including "[[I Will Always Love You]]"{{snd}}a two-time U.S. country chart-topper and an [[I Will Always Love You (Whitney Houston recording)|international success]] for [[Whitney Houston]] that became the [[List of best-selling singles|best-selling single by a woman]]{{snd}}"[[Jolene]]", "[[Coat of Many Colors (song)|Coat of Many Colors]]", and the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] number-one single "[[9 to 5 (Dolly Parton song)|9{{spaces}}to{{spaces}}5]]". She also recorded the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 number‑one single "[[Islands in the Stream (song)|Islands in the Stream]]", a duet with [[Kenny Rogers]]. Her final solo studio album, ''[[Rockstar (Dolly Parton album)|Rockstar]]'' (2023), became her highest-charting album on the [[Billboard 200|''Billboard'' 200]], reaching number three.

Onscreen, Parton starred in ''[[9 to 5 (film)|9 to 5]]'' (1980) and ''[[The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas (film)|The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas]]'' (1982), both earning her nominations for [[Golden Globe Award for Best Actress – Motion Picture Comedy or Musical|Golden Globe]], as well as ''[[Rhinestone (film)|Rhinestone]]'' (1984), ''[[Steel Magnolias]]'' (1989), ''[[Straight Talk]]'' (1992), and ''[[Joyful Noise (film)|Joyful Noise]]'' (2012). On television, she played [[Aunt Dolly]] in ''[[Hannah Montana]]'' (2006–2010), hosted ''[[Saturday Night Live]]'' (1989), and guest-starred on ''[[Reba (TV series)|Reba]]'' (2005) and ''[[Grace and Frankie]]'' (2022). She produced and starred in the [[Netflix]] film ''[[Christmas on the Square]]'' (2021), winning a [[Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Movie|Primetime Emmy Award]]. On [[Broadway (theatre)|Broadway]], she wrote the music and lyrics for the musical ''[[9 to 5 (musical)|9 to 5]]'' (2009), for which she was nominated for the [[Tony Award for Best Original Score]]. Her life will be depicted in ''[[Dolly: A True Original Musical]]'' (2026).

Parton's music received gold, platinum, and multi-platinum certifications from the [[Recording Industry Association of America]] (RIAA). [[List of awards and nominations received by Dolly Parton|Her accolades]] include eleven [[Grammy Awards]] and three [[Emmy Awards]], as well as nominations for two [[Academy Awards]], six [[Golden Globes]] and a [[Tony Award]]. She logged 25 number-one ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' country singles (tied with [[Reba McEntire]] for the most by a woman), 44 career [[Top Country Albums|top-10 country albums]] (a record for any artist), and 110 career-charted singles over 40 years. Parton was honored with a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] (1984), the [[National Medal of Arts]] (2004), the [[Kennedy Center Honor]] (2006), the [[Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award]] (2011) and the [[Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award]] (2025).
